newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NBNZ economists recommend lower govt spending.
newsitem.headline: NBNZ economists recommend lower govt spending.

text.p: National Bank of New Zealand Ltd economists warned on Wednesday of a slide back into a "traditional Kiwi business cycle" and urged the centre-right coalition government to cut spending.
They said the traditional cycle was "a short-lived boost to government spending, leaving investment, employment and exports in its wake".
In the past this had led to high inflation, rising government debt and/or a blowout in the external deficit.
The NBNZ economists, in their February business outlook, expressed concern about the new coalition government's pledge to spend an extra NZ$5 billion over the next three years.

"An increase in government spending in an economy near its potential growth limit will raise interest rates and the exchange rate. This costs investment and exports," NBNZ said, citing the growing current account deficit as evidence.
The current account deficit stood at 4.6 percent of Gross Domestic Product at September 30, 1996.

To date, it has mainly reflected investment rather than consumption spending, but NBNZ said that over the next couple of years, government and household consumer imports would replace business investment and raise questions about the country's future ability to honour its debt.

The bank's economists said economic stability could be jeopardised if monetary policy was constantly forced to lean against government-fuelled inflation. It cited the 1994/95 Mexican peso crisis to illustrate the perils of overheating the domestic economy at the expense of the external sectors.
Chief Economist Adrian Orr said raising national savings would reduce such a risk in New Zealand, but was unlikely to occur with the current coalition government's policies.
"Increased government spending and reduced incentives for the self-provision of education, health and retirement income may instead lead to a further decline in savings," he said.
"In the absence of any reforms, raising government saving is the most effective and efficient means of improving national savings, while also reducing the current business cycle pressures."
